summary: Discusses what an Internet standard data link protocol for point-to-point links should be able to do and how to judge candidates. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1547 is the checklist that a standard protocol for carrying IP over a telephone-line or serial connection would have to pass. It lists what such a protocol must do, what it must deliberately not do, and why the protocols that already existed each fell short.

questions: what are the requirements for a point-to-point protocol
what features does a point-to-point protocol need
what is an internet standard point-to-point protocol
subtitle: The 1989 checklist that any standard protocol for point-to-point links had to satisfy.

tldr.problem: There were plenty of ways to carry IP over a serial line, but none of them was agreed as an Internet Standard, and each proposal had been built to solve one narrow problem.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1547 sets out seventeen features a standard point-to-point protocol must have, seven it must deliberately leave out, and then checks the existing protocols against the list to show where each one falls short.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that specifies no standard of any kind. Its abstract records that it was the design requirements document of June 1989, followed by RFC 1134, and that it is published for completeness and future guidance.

today: RFC 1547 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard of any kind, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its abstract carries a historical note that it was the design requirements document of June 1989, followed by RFC 1134, and that it is published for completeness and future guidance. Its Security Consideration says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

sections.title: Why a Standard Point-to-Point Protocol Was Needed
sections.content:
The memo starts from the growth of the Internet. The number of hosts supporting IP had grown explosively, and the vast majority were attached to local area networks of various types, Ethernet being the most common, while most of the others were connected through wide area networks such as X.25-style public data networks. Far fewer were connected by simple point-to-point links, even though point-to-point serial links are among the oldest methods of data communications and almost every host supports them; asynchronous RS-232 interfaces were essentially ubiquitous.

One reason for the small number of point-to-point IP links was the lack of a single established encapsulation protocol. There were plenty of non-standard, and at least one de facto standard, encapsulation protocols available, but none had been agreed on as an Internet Standard. A number of protocols had been proposed to the Internet community, but no consensus was reached on which to adopt, and the memo suggests a reason: these proposals often addressed specific problems rather than providing a general purpose service. The example it gives is Rick Adams' SLIP protocol for BSD UNIX, which provides only the most rudimentary support for sending IP datagrams over asynchronous serial lines and ignores issues such as the use of protocols other than IP and the use of synchronous links.

The purpose of the document is to propose a set of requirements for an Internet Standard point-to-point protocol. It is not proposing any one design for the standard; any solutions outlined in the text are intended only as examples and do not preclude other implementations. The document has four major sections: definitions of the technical terms, the proposed requirements with the issues other protocols ignore, a set of non-requirements, and an analysis of existing protocols against the requirements.

The abstract carries a historical note: this was the design requirements document dated June 1989, which was followed for RFC 1134 through the present, and it is now published for completeness and future guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: Many people had invented ways of sending IP down a serial line, but each was built for one situation and none was agreed as the standard. This memo is the answer to the question: what would a standard protocol have to do?

sections.title: The Features a Standard Protocol Must Have
sections.content:
The requirements are chosen so that the standard protocol serves the needs of its users. Some needs are universal, such as packet framing, which the memo calls a fundamental necessity; others are specific and may even conflict, since determining whether a connection is alive is very important on some links and very expensive on others. A standard protocol must address all of them and resolve the conflicts.

The way conflicts are resolved is itself a requirement. A protocol feature must have both an enabled and a disabled mode, and the two modes must be compatible with each other. The enabled mode solves problems where they exist, the disabled mode lets them be ignored where they do not, and implementations are required to support both and to let the user, which need not be a person, choose dynamically. The memo notes that this is the same solution used by UDP, whose datagram checksum may be computed or not, with compatibility maintained by requiring the checksum to be sent as zero in the disabled mode and ignored when received as zero in either mode.

The seventeen requirements themselves are these. The protocol must be simple, because the Internet architecture puts the most complexity in the transport layer, IP is a fairly simple almost stateless protocol, and a simple design decreases the incidence of programming errors and so increases the likelihood of interoperability. It must be transparent to higher layers, placing no constraints on transmitted data and carrying everything unmodified end to end, which means it must be able to disambiguate higher level data from its own framing characters, by escaping or bit stuffing. It must frame packets correctly and efficiently, so that a receiver can find the beginning and end of each packet, the boundary of each octet, and each bit within an octet.

It must use bandwidth efficiently, so that the overhead imposes at most a few percent reduction in raw link bandwidth, and it must process its headers very fast, with a very simple format for data packets in the normal case and without complex field checking. It must multiplex many higher level protocols, since IP networks often have to support AppleTalk, DECnet, IPX and XNS, and for that it needs a protocol type field; sixteen bits are suggested, although twelve bits, giving 4096 protocols, should suffice. It must support a multiplicity of physical and data link layer protocols and must not inhibit any type of link, including asynchronous, bit-oriented synchronous links such as HDLC and X.25 LAPB, and byte-oriented synchronous links such as BISYNC and DDCMP; at first it must support full duplex asynchronous RS-232 links with 8 bits of data and no parity, from 300 to 19.2k bps or more, and full duplex bit-oriented synchronous links including RS-422, RS-423, V.35 and T1.

It must provide some form of basic error detection, since a checksum or CRC prevents wasted bandwidth from propagating corrupted packets, though link level error correction is not required. It must have a standardised default maximum packet length for each kind of link, at least 1500 bytes to carry common LAN traffic efficiently; higher layers must not transmit more, and a packet that is too long must be dropped with an error returned. It must support both switched and non-switched links, such as a three-wire RS-232 cable on one side and a voice network or ISDN on the other, although procedures for establishing switched connections are out of scope. It should operate symmetrically, because pre-assigned static roles such as master and slave destroy symmetry, though roles may be determined dynamically per connection.

It must include a mechanism to determine automatically when a link is functioning properly and when it is defunct, enabled by default but always disableable, which should discover changes in status within no more than a few minutes. Continuing to use a link that is down causes routing problems commonly called black holes, which are hard to find and diagnose. A link is defined to be down at initialisation, and its liveness must be verified before it may be declared up, which means both ends must be able to transmit and receive. This feature may be disabled where determining status is expensive, such as a link that traverses a public data network such as TELENET or TYMNET, where constant pinging would be charged for.

It must detect a looped-back link automatically, without operator assistance and in no longer than one period of the liveness protocol, and while the link is looped each end must declare the other unreachable. It must detect misconfigured connections quickly, and a misconfigured connection must never be declared up; because many systems, gateways in particular, have more than one point-to-point connection and cables are easily plugged into the wrong connector, the protocol should verify the remote end's identity whenever possible before marking an interface as operational, for the detection of simple errors rather than rigorous authentication.

It must allow network layer addresses to be negotiated, by an algorithm as simple as possible that is guaranteed to terminate, which matters for switched media, where a dial-up IP gateway must know the address of its peer before packets can be routed. It must provide a way to negotiate data compression, also simple and guaranteed to terminate; the protocol need not standardise any compression algorithm, a conforming implementation may refuse to compress when negotiating, refusal always takes precedence over an offer, several independent schemes may be used at once, and the negotiation must distinguish between different algorithms so that compression is not enabled unless the same algorithm is used at both ends.

Finally it must allow for future extensions in a flexible way, since the Internet will never cease to evolve. A proposed solution is to specify an option negotiation protocol, which could be used for negotiating network layer addresses, compression schemes, the maximum packet length and encryption, and which must itself be extensible, allowing the negotiation of a large number of future options and the use of other types of link and encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is long but the idea is simple: the protocol must do the small number of things a link has to do, must do them quickly, and must be able to be told to leave out anything that is not needed on a particular line. It also has to notice when the line is broken, when it is plugged into the wrong socket, and when it is talking to itself.

sections.title: The Features It Must Not Have
sections.content:
Some functionality is explicitly not required, though it may be included as long as it does not break any of the requirements.

Error correction is the responsibility of the transport layer and is not required, though on links with high error rates performance may be better with error correction at the data link layer, so the protocol must not prevent it being added by private agreement. Flow control, such as XON/XOFF, is not required, because any implementation is expected to be able to receive packets at the full rate the link allows; if higher layers cannot keep up it is up to them to discard packets or invoke flow control, and including flow control in the link protocol often violates the requirement for simplicity. Sequencing is not required either: the protocol need provide no more service than IP, an unreliable datagram service free to reorder packets, and it is specifically allowed to reorder packets according to a type of service criterion in a higher layer.

There is no requirement for backward compatibility with any other point-to-point protocol, because there are no official Internet Standards with which compatibility must be maintained, and attempting it might impose needless restrictions on the new protocol; there is, however, no need for the designers to go out of their way to inhibit it.

Multi-point links are not required, because many of the features that are required are only valid between two peers, and the benefits of supporting them are outweighed by the added complexity. A historical note records that the original rationale also said it was unlikely many new types of multi-point link would be introduced in the foreseeable future, and that since then considerable effort has been expended on new multi-point links, including Switched Multimegabit Data Service, Frame Relay and Asynchronous Transfer Mode, but that it is clear these are considerably more complex than the standard protocol the memo envisages.

Support for half-duplex or simplex links is not required, because those types are not in common use in the current Internet and half-duplex links need some method of turning the line around; such support might be added later through the required extension mechanism. And the use of asynchronous RS-232 need not support 7-bit links, because 8-bit links are predominant and supporting 7-bit links introduces unnecessary complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is as careful about what to leave out. A link protocol should not retransmit data, should not slow the sender down, and should not care about ordering, because the transport layer above already does all of that. Doing it twice would waste effort and slow everything down.

sections.title: The Internet Protocols That Fall Short
sections.content:
The memo then checks the existing protocols against the requirements. Appendix A of RFC 891, DCN Local-Network Protocols, describes the data link formats used by the Fuzzball system for asynchronous, character-oriented synchronous, DDCMP, HDLC, ARPANET 1822, X.25 LAPB and ethernet links. These meet the requirements for simplicity, transparency, packet framing and efficiency, but fall short of many of the others: most assume IP and include no protocol demultiplexing field, no error detection is provided except where another standard requires it, the MTU used for any of these links is not mentioned, loopback and misconfiguration detection are not discussed, and no option negotiation scheme is defined, which without a demultiplexing field would be difficult or impossible to include.

RFC 914, Thinwire Protocols, places its main emphasis on decreasing round-trip delay and increasing link efficiency with header compression rather than data compression, and discusses three protocols, Thinwire I, Thinwire II and Thinwire III. The latter two require a reliable data link layer protocol, and the one proposed in its Appendix D is not Rick Adams' SLIP. It does not meet many of the requirements: although not terribly complex, as a reliable, error detecting and correcting protocol it is not simple; the 32 octet packet size makes it inefficient for large or uncompressed packets, requiring complex fragmentation and reassembly; the use of links other than asynchronous is not mentioned; the entire reliable link layer would be redundant over LAPB links; and there is no mechanism for option negotiation or future extensibility.

RFC 916 presents RATP, the Reliable Asynchronous Transfer Protocol, which provides error detection and correction, sequencing and flow control across a point-to-point connection, and is directed at full duplex RS-232 links. The memo judges it far from simple: it solves many of the problems labelled non-requirements and fails to solve many stated requirements. It does not support option negotiation and has no mechanism for future extensibility, and since it was published no consensus has emerged advocating it, so RATP is not recommended.

RFC 935 is a rebuttal to the protocols proposed in RFCs 914 and 916. It discusses existing and widely used national and international standards, including character-oriented asynchronous and synchronous protocols and bit-oriented synchronous protocols, but presents no higher level issues such as option negotiation or extensibility. Section 3 of RFC 1009 briefly discusses requirements for transmitting IP datagrams over a number of types of point-to-point link, naming X.25 LAPB, HDLC framed synchronous links, Xerox Synchronous Point-to-Point synchronous lines and the MIT Serial Line Framing Protocol, but only mentions them as reasonable candidates and does not go into depth.

RFC 1055, Rick Adams' Serial Line IP, has become something of a de facto standard because of the popularity of the 4.2 and 4.3BSD UNIX operating systems; it is easily added to 4.2 systems and included with 4.3, and many other TCP/IP implementations added it to stay compatible, though before RFC 1055 it was specified only in the source code. SLIP meets the requirement for simplicity and also those for transparency and bandwidth efficiency, but it only provides for sending IP packets over asynchronous serial lines, and since it provides no higher level protocol field for demultiplexing it cannot support multiple concurrent higher level protocols. Providing only a framing protocol it would be entirely redundant over a LAPB synchronous link, it includes absolutely no mechanism for error detection, not even parity, and for the same reason it supports no option negotiation or extensibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo goes through the candidates one at a time. The recurring gaps are the same: no way to tell which protocol is inside a packet, no way to notice a bad or missing link, and no way to agree on extra features when the link comes up.

sections.title: The International Standards and the Vendor Protocols
sections.content:
Among the international protocols, ISO 3309, the HDLC frame structure, is a simple data link layer protocol providing framing of packets over bit-oriented synchronous links; special flag sequences mark the beginning and end of frames, bit stuffing allows data containing flag characters to be transmitted, and a 16-bit Frame Check Sequence provides error detection. By itself it meets most requirements: it does not provide protocol multiplexing, standard MTUs, fault detection or option negotiation, and there is no mechanism for future extensibility. Given its wide acceptance and simplicity, the memo says it may be an ideal building block for the standard protocol.

ISO 6256, the HDLC Balanced Class of Procedures, specifies a data link layer protocol providing error correction, sequencing and flow control, building on ISO 3309 and ISO 4335. It provides no more utility against the requirements than ISO 3309 does, because the capabilities it adds are all considered unnecessary and overly complex. CCITT X.25 describes a network layer protocol providing error-free, sequenced, flow controlled virtual circuits, and includes a data link layer, X.25 LAPB, which uses ISO 3309, 4335 and 6256; neither meets any more of the requirements than the ISO protocols do. CCITT I.441 LAPD defines the Link Access Procedure on the ISDN D-Channel, and its data link layer is very similar to LAPB and fails to meet the same requirements.

The vendor protocols are described next. The Cisco Systems gateway supports asynchronous links using SLIP and synchronous links using simple HDLC framing, X.25 LAPB or full X.25. Its HDLC framing procedure includes a four byte header: the first octet, an address, is either 0x0F for unicast intent or 0x8F for multicast intent; the second octet, a control byte, is left zero and is not checked on reception; and the third and fourth octets carry a standard 16-bit Ethernet protocol type code. A keepalive or beaconing protocol ensures two-way connectivity, with each end periodically sending two 32-bit sequence numbers, its own and the one received from the other side, so hearing its own number back shows the link works in both directions. The keepalive protocol is extensible, and one extension defaults IP addresses on serial lines of systems without non-volatile memory.

The MIT PC/IP framing protocol provides a mechanism for transmitting IP datagrams over asynchronous links, with a low-level protocol sublayer providing encapsulation and a local net protocol providing multiplexing of IP datagrams and IP address request packets. It only allows host-to-gateway connections, and host-to-gateway flow control is provided by requiring the host to transmit request packets until an acknowledgment is received. It does not implement error detection, connection status determination, fault detection or option negotiation, and supports only asynchronous links.

The Proteon p4200 router supports transmission of packets over bit-oriented synchronous links at speeds from zero to 2 Mb/sec. Its protocol encapsulates packets inside HDLC frames but does not use the HDLC address or control fields, using those two octets instead for a 16-bit type field, and it does use the HDLC frame check sequence trailer. Its protocol type numbers are ad hoc and correspond to no existing standard, and a simple liveness protocol detects dead connections. It meets many of the requirements but not option negotiation. The Ungermann Bass router supports synchronous links using simple HDLC framing, with neither the HDLC address nor the control field used and IP datagrams placed immediately after the HDLC flag; it meets none of the requirements for fault detection or option negotiation, and defines no mechanism for future extensibility. The Wellfleet router also uses simple HDLC framing, using the HDLC address and placing the Unnumbered Information command in all frames, with a simple header after the UI command providing a two octet type field using the same values as Ethernet; it too fails the fault detection and option negotiation requirements, and defines no extensibility mechanism, although one could be added.

The Xerox Network Systems Synchronous Point-to-Point protocol was designed to address most of the same issues, and it meets the requirements for simplicity, transparency, efficiency, packet framing, protocol multiplexing, error detection, standard MTUs, symmetry, switched and non-switched media, connection status, network address negotiation and future extensibility. It does not meet the requirements for multiple data link layer protocols, fault detection and data compression negotiation, and although it provides protocol multiplexing its packet type field has only 8 bits, which is too few.
sections.plainLanguage: The same gaps show up in the commercial protocols too. Nearly all of them can carry an IP packet over a serial line, and nearly all of them have no way to say which protocol is inside the packet, no way to notice a dead line, and no way to agree on options when the link comes up.

sections.title: Security and the Standing of the Memo
sections.content:
The memo closes with a Security Consideration that is one sentence long: security issues are not discussed in it. The requirements themselves touch on security only obliquely, in the requirement to verify the remote end's identity before marking an interface as operational, and the memo is careful to say that this is the detection of simple errors rather than rigorous authentication.

The standing of the document is set out in the abstract, which records that this was the design requirements document dated June 1989, that it was followed for RFC 1134 through the present, and that it is now published for completeness and future guidance. The memo states that it specifies no Internet standard of any kind, and that any solutions outlined in the text are examples that do not preclude other implementations.

The back matter names the working group's chair, Fred Baker of Advanced Computer Communications, gives the author's address at Carnegie Mellon University, and records that the typographic revision and the historical notes were done by William Allen Simpson.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says nothing about security, and it describes itself as a historical document published for guidance. The protocol it imagines would check who is on the other end of the line well enough to catch a mis-wired cable, but not well enough to be trusted.

cells: Simplicity
No more capability than IP provides; no error correction, sequencing or flow control, which would duplicate the transport layer.
Transparency
No constraints on transmitted data, which must be carried unmodified end to end, with framing characters disambiguated by escaping or bit stuffing.
Packet framing
A receiver must find the start and end of each packet, the boundary of each octet, and each bit within an octet.
Bandwidth efficiency
Overhead may take at most a few percent off the raw link bandwidth.
Protocol multiplexing
A protocol type field so that several higher level protocols can share the link; 16 bits are suggested, 12 should suffice.
Many kinds of link
Must not inhibit asynchronous, bit-oriented synchronous or byte-oriented synchronous links; first support RS-232, RS-422, RS-423, V.35 and T1.
Error detection
Some basic form, such as a checksum or CRC, to stop corrupted packets wasting bandwidth. Error correction is not required.
Standard MTU
A default maximum packet length per link type of at least 1500 bytes; a longer packet must be dropped with an error.
Connection liveness
Automatic detection of a dead link within a few minutes, enabled by default but always disableable.
Loopback detection
A looped link detected without operator assistance, in no longer than one liveness period.
Misconfiguration detection
A misconfigured connection must never be declared up; the remote end's identity is verified where possible.
Address and compression negotiation
Both negotiable by a simple algorithm guaranteed to terminate, with refusal of compression taking precedence over an offer.
Extensibility
An extensible option negotiation protocol, usable for addresses, compression, the MTU and encryption.

viz.caption: THE FEATURES THAT ARE EXPLICITLY NOT REQUIRED

items.title: Error correction
items.text: The transport layer's job. The protocol must not prevent it being added by private agreement on a noisy link.

items.title: Flow control
items.text: Not required, because implementations should already be able to receive at the full rate the link allows.

items.title: Sequencing
items.text: Not required. The protocol need provide no more service than IP, which is free to reorder packets.

items.title: Backward compatibility
items.text: Not required, since there is no official Internet Standard to be compatible with, and the restriction would limit the new design.

items.title: Multi-point links
items.text: Not required, because many required features only make sense between two peers, and the complexity would outweigh the benefit.

items.title: Half-duplex and simplex links
items.text: Not required; they are not in common use, and no line turn-around mechanism is needed.

items.title: 7-bit RS-232 links
items.text: Not required; 8-bit links are predominant, and supporting 7-bit links adds unnecessary complexity.

viz.caption: WHERE THE EXISTING PROTOCOLS FALL SHORT

cells: RFC 891, DCN Local-Network Protocols
Framing for many kinds of link, meeting the simplicity, transparency and efficiency requirements
Assumes IP with no demultiplexing field, no error detection, no MTU, no loopback or misconfiguration detection, no option negotiation
RFC 914, Thinwire
Low delay and high link efficiency through header compression
Not simple; a 32 octet packet size is inefficient; asynchronous links only; no option negotiation or extensibility
RFC 916, RATP
Error detection and correction, sequencing and flow control
Far from simple, solving what the memo calls non-requirements; no option negotiation or extensibility; not recommended
RFC 1055, SLIP
Simple, transparent and bandwidth efficient for IP over asynchronous serial lines
IP only; no protocol type field; no error detection at all; no option negotiation or extensibility
ISO 3309, HDLC framing
Simple framing with flags, bit stuffing and a 16-bit frame check sequence
No multiplexing, no standard MTU, no fault detection, no option negotiation, no extensibility
XNS Synchronous Point-to-Point
Meets most of the requirements, including extensibility and address negotiation
No multiple data link protocols, no fault detection, no compression negotiation; an 8-bit type field is too few
Proteon p4200
Encapsulates packets in HDLC frames with a 16-bit type field and a liveness protocol
Protocol type numbers are ad hoc; no option negotiation
